fixes.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says Paul “…was permitted to stay by himself, with a soldier to guard him.” (Acts 28:16) He's still a prisoner, since a soldier guards him. But he gets to stay by himself. I think that's a lot better than what I'd have expected for a prisoner.
That's the one. The text says they found brothers “…who invited us to spend the week with them.” (Acts 28:14) Fellow believers, and they invite the group to stay. A good host is a gift, friend.

Nobody gets shooed down the road here. The brothers invited the group to spend the week with them, and only after that does the text say, “And so we came to Rome.” (Acts 28:14) The stop in Puteoli came first. A week with the brothers before Rome sounds good to me.

Yes, baker. Paul says the Romans “…examined me and wanted to release me, because there was no basis for a death sentence against me.” (Acts 28:18) They looked into it and wanted him released. I've had cookies inspected before, and I never got a verdict that clean.

No island in that plan, baker. Paul says the Romans “…wanted to release me, because there was no basis for a death sentence against me.” (Acts 28:18) Paul did end up on an island, Malta (Acts 28:1), after the ship broke apart (Acts 27:41–44). But that's not what the Romans wanted for him. What they wanted was to let him go.

Paul does mention a chain in verse 20, but that's not what the Romans wanted. He says they “…wanted to release me, because there was no basis for a death sentence against me.” (Acts 28:18) So they wanted him free, not kept in chains.

Not quite, baker. Paul says he was compelled to appeal to Caesar, “…even though I have no charge to bring against my nation.” (Acts 28:19) He's telling the leaders he has no charge against his own nation. He says he was compelled to appeal when the Jews objected.

False is right. Paul says he was compelled to appeal to Caesar, “…even though I have no charge to bring against my nation.” (Acts 28:19) He has no charge to bring against his nation. What he says is that when the Jews objected, he was compelled to appeal.

That's his answer, baker, and he doesn't dodge it. “It is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.” (Acts 28:20) No crime on his list, just the hope of Israel. I bet he'd say that one out loud all day.

Not quite, baker. Paul says he was compelled to appeal to Caesar (Acts 28:19). That's an appeal, and he says nothing here about speaking against him. The reason he gives for the chain is, “It is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.” (Acts 28:20)

They say it plainly: “…we consider your views worth hearing…” (Acts 28:22). The leaders tell Paul they've received no letters about him from Judea, and none of the brothers from there reported or mentioned anything bad about him (Acts 28:21). So they're willing to listen to him themselves. Not a bad way to open a conversation.

Not Roman teachers, friend. The text says Paul was “…persuading them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets.” (Acts 28:23) That's what he persuaded them from. He also spent from morning to evening testifying about the kingdom of God.

True. Paul says the Holy Spirit spoke through Isaiah the prophet (Acts 28:25), and those words say, “Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.” (Acts 28:27) Seeing, hearing, understanding and turning come first. Then comes the healing.

It's true, friend. Paul says the Holy Spirit spoke through Isaiah the prophet (Acts 28:25), and those words say, “Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.” (Acts 28:27) The healing comes with seeing, hearing, understanding and turning. It's right there in the verse.

Not the Pharisees, baker. Paul says, “Be advised, therefore, that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen!” (Acts 28:28) He doesn't name the Pharisees here. The word is Gentiles, people who aren't Jewish.
